## Question 1

***Assumptions***

1.  The data is made up of basic random values drawn from the population

2.  First, we test the hypothesis of normality of the dependent variable therefore the price of diamonds

```{r, echo=FALSE}
shapiro.test(diamonds$price[1:5000])
```

Since the p-value < 2.2e-16, implies that data distribution don't follows the normal distribution.

3.  Next, we will test the hypothesis of equality of variances between the groups.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
bartlett.test(diamonds$price ~ diamonds$cut)
```

Since the p-value< 2.2e-16, implies that the variances don't to be equal.

***ANOVA***

Let m1, m2, m3, m4 and m5 respectively be the mean prices of diamonds which group are "Ideal", "Premium", "Good", "Very Good", and "Fair".

H0: m1=m2=m3=m4=m5 
Ha: At least one mean different

```{r, echo=FALSE}
oneway.test(price ~ cut, data = diamonds, var.equal = FALSE)
```

*Conclusion*

With an alpha of 0.05, and a p-value< 2.2e-16, we reject the null and stat that we have sufficient evidence to show that there was a effect of cut on diamond prices.

# Question 2

The hypotheses are:

-   H0: m1=m2=m3=m4=m5

-   Ha: At least one mean different

```{r, echo=FALSE}
oneway.test(price ~ cut, data = diamonds, var.equal = TRUE)
```

There is no obvious difference in p-value but the F-statistic is different as well as "num df" and "denom df".

# Question 3

```{r, echo=FALSE}
diamonds["cut_labelled"]=factor(diamonds$cut, levels = c("Ideal","Premium","Good","Very Good","Fair"), labels = c("I","P","G","VG","F"))
model<-aov(price ~ cut_labelled, data = diamonds)
TUKEY<-TukeyHSD(model, conf.level=0.95)
TUKEY
```

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.height=8, echo=FALSE}
plot(TUKEY)
```

***Interpretations***

The average price of diamonds in the "Premium", "Good", "Very Good", "Fair" categories is significantly higher than that of the "Ideal" category (with estimated difference of 1126.71573, 471.32248, 524.21792, 901.21579 respectively and p-value of 0.0 for all)

The average price of diamonds in the "Premium" category is significantly higher than in the "Good" and "Very Good" categories (with estimated difference of 655.39325, 602.49781 respectively and p-value of 0.0 for all).

The average price of diamonds in the "Fair" category is significantly higher than in the "Good" and "Very Good" categories (with estimated difference of 429.89331, 376.99787 respectively and p-value of 0.0014980 and 0.0031094 respectively.


# Question 4

The hypotheses are:

-   H0: m3=m4

-   Ha: m3!=m4

```{r, echo=FALSE}
## Extraction and delete cut_labelled column 
df <- subset(diamonds, cut %in% c("Good", "Very Good"), select=-c(cut_labelled))
## Perform one way ANOVA
oneway.test(price ~ cut, data = df, var.equal = TRUE)
```

*Conclusion*

With an alpha of 0.05, and a p-value of 0.4188, we fail to reject the null and stat that we have insufficient evidence to show that there was a cut effect of on diamond prices.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
TUKEY
```


# Question 6

```{r, echo=FALSE}
df <- subset(diamonds, select = c("cut","carat","color","depth","price"))
df$cut<- as.factor(df$cut)
df$color<- as.factor(df$color)
lr<-lm(price~cut+color+carat+depth, data = df)
summary(lr)
```
The coefficient of determination is 0.8713, which indicates that the model accounts for 87.13% of the variation in the diamond price.
- An increase of one unit of depth results in a decrease of 35.979 in the diamond 
- An increase of one unit of carat results in a increase of 8183.774 in the diamond price.
- If the item is in the "Ideal" category, there is an increase of 1177.948 in the diamond price. A decrease of 491.180 for "Premium", an increase of 370.82 for "Good", an increase of 85.419 for "Very Good".

# Question 7

```{r, echo=FALSE}
fitAll <- lm(price ~ ., data = subset(diamonds, select = -c(cut_labelled)))

lr.final <- step(fitAll, direction = "forward")

summary(lr.final)
```

***Conclusion***

The determination coefficient of the R-squared model is 0.9198. This indicates that the model expresses 91.98% of the variation in diamond prices.

# Question 8

```{r, echo=FALSE}
set.seed(2)
df<-df[sample(nrow(df), 1000), ]
lr<-lm(price~cut+color+carat+depth, data = df)
plot(lr)
```
***Interpretation***

There is a predefined light parabolic shape on one side of the Residuals vs Fitted graph.
This tells us that the model is incomplete: it is missing a quadratic factor that could explain a larger variation in diamond prices.
The normal Q - Q plot has enough points off the line, this indicates that the residuals do not follow a normal distribution.
The points 785 and 905 stand out on each of the plots, this indicates that there is a problem with these observations.
